title: a boy who wouldn't wear the thread
hook: a boy who wouldn't wear the thread; a man who walked for twenty years
carry: there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim
tomorrow: the first symbol of the scripture

segments.voice: Yesterday: Waheguru. Wahe, wow. Guru, the teacher. Your line was just wow. What was the one thing that earned it? Day three.

A village in Punjab, more than five hundred years ago. The family has gathered, the priest has come, and there's food for the guests. It's a big day for a boy, about eleven in the traditional telling: the ceremony where he'll receive a sacred thread, a cotton cord worn over the shoulder, a mark of his family's high place in the world. The priest sits him down and reaches for the thread. And the boy asks a question nobody expected. What is this thread for? And will it last? Everybody waits. Tradition says the boy politely refused to wear it. That boy grew up to be the first Guru of the Sikhs, and his name is today's word.
screen: `A FAMILY, A PRIEST, A SACRED THREAD.` → `WHAT IS THIS FOR?` → `THE BOY SAYS NO.`

segments.voice: Nanak. Guru Nanak, born, tradition says, in 1469, in a village called Talwandi, in what's now Pakistan. Everything on this path starts with him. Here's how the story of the thread goes on. Nanak wasn't being rude. He told the priest he'd gladly wear a thread, just a different one. In one of his own hymns, now in the Sikh scripture, he describes it: let compassion be the cotton, contentment the thread, self-control the knots, and truth the twist. A thread like that, he says, doesn't break, doesn't get dirty, doesn't burn, and isn't lost. That's Nanak in miniature. He didn't mock the ritual. He asked what it was pointing at, and then he went straight there. And then he walked. As a grown man, Nanak set out on long journeys, and tradition says they lasted over twenty years. On foot, across India and, the stories say, as far as Tibet, Sri Lanka, Mecca and Baghdad. His companion was a Muslim musician named Mardana, who played while Nanak sang. They visited Hindu holy places and Muslim ones, sat with yogis and Sufis and ordinary villagers, and kept asking the same kind of question he asked about the thread. What is this for? What's underneath it? Your line today comes from the moment his mission began. After an experience we'll come to later in the path, the first words he's remembered saying were: there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim. People have heard that in more than one way. Some hear it as: beneath the labels, there are just people, all made by the one God. Others hear a challenge: nobody was truly living up to the name they carried. Both readings are told. And both sound like the boy with the thread.
screen: `GURU NANAK, THE FIRST GURU.` · `COMPASSION FOR COTTON, TRUTH FOR THE TWIST.` · `TWENTY YEARS ON FOOT, WITH MARDANA.` · `THERE IS NO HINDU, THERE IS NO MUSLIM.` · then, large: `WHAT IS THIS FOR?`

segments.voice: Three breaths, with the bell. Think of one thing you do by habit: a ritual, a routine, something you've done so often you've stopped noticing. On the first breath, picture it. On the second, ask Nanak's question: what is this for? On the third, let the answer come, even if it's only half an answer.
Nanak. Guru Nanak, the first Guru of the Sikhs, who asked what things were for, and walked for twenty years. Third word.
Your line: there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim. Today, when you meet someone, try seeing the person first and the label second. Day three.

howItsDone: Sikhs honor Guru Nanak as the first of ten Gurus and celebrate his birth each year with a festival, readings of the scripture and langar; his hymns open the Guru Granth Sahib.

fork.setup: you're eleven. your family has gathered and the priest is holding out the sacred thread. what do you do?
options: put it on and enjoy the party.
ask what it's for, and ask for a thread that won't break.
fork.reveal: tradition says Nanak asked for a thread of compassion, contentment, self-control and truth, one that never breaks, burns or gets lost.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: the name of the first Guru, which he also uses to sign his own hymns.

trapdoor: what you thought: the founder of a religion.
what it means: the first Guru, who kept asking what rituals were for, walked for years among people of every faith, and taught one God beneath the labels.
what a scholar hears: Nanak signs his hymns with his own name, and the later Gurus whose hymns sit beside his signed theirs as Nanak too, so a line signed Nanak may come from any of them.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 471 (Asa di Var: the thread of compassion, contentment, self-control and truth)

notes: The janeu (sacred thread) story: age about eleven per common tradition; the hymn is in Asa di Var, Ang 471. The janamsakhi setting of the hymn at the ceremony is traditional. Confirm the Ang and the age.
Journeys (udasis): the length ('over twenty years') and destinations (Tibet, Sri Lanka, Mecca, Baghdad) are from tradition; framed as 'tradition says' and 'the stories say'. Confirm.
Two readings of 'there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim' are given without ranking; confirm both are fairly described. The full story is day 29.
The validator warns that the carry has capitals ('Hindu', 'Muslim'); the carry is kept exactly as the index gives it, and proper nouns need capitals.
Trapdoor floor 3: the later Gurus composed under the name Nanak (identified by Mahala numbers). Confirm wording.

Editor review (2026-10-01): birth year and the boy's age now framed as tradition; 1469 removed from the word segment, a teach head and a match pair (replaced with Talwandi); 'many Sikhs hear it as' softened to 'some hear it as'; trapdoor narrowed from 'the Gurus who came after him' (Guru Gobind Singh's writings are not in the Guru Granth Sahib) to 'the later Gurus whose hymns sit beside his'.
